entities.summary:
Metrodorus of Lampsacus was a Greek philosopher of the Epicurean school, born in Lampsacus, Pontus, during the Hellenistic period. Although one of the four major proponents of Epicureanism, only fragments of his works remain. A Metrodorus bust was found in Velia, slightly different modeled to depict Parmenides.

Metrodorus' philosophical contributions were heavily influenced by the works of Democritus and Epicurus, which emphasized the importance of reason, individualism, and the rejection of supernatural beliefs. His ideas about the nature of the soul and the afterlife were particularly influential, and his concept of the 'common table' – a shared communal space for Epicureans to engage in philosophical discussions – became a central aspect of Epicurean thought.

Metrodorus' significance extends beyond the realm of philosophy, as his ideas about the importance of individualism and the rejection of supernatural beliefs resonated with the cultural and intellectual currents of ancient Greece. His influence can be seen in the works of later philosophers, such as Lucretius and Sextus Empiricus, who built upon his ideas and expanded their scope. Metrodorus' legacy continues to be felt in modern Western philosophy, where his emphasis on reason, individualism, and the scientific method remains a cornerstone of Epicurean thought.

The discovery of the Metrodorus bust in Velia in 1963 provided a significant insight into the life and work of this enigmatic philosopher, shedding light on the cultural and intellectual context in which he lived and thought. The bust, now housed at the British Museum, serves as a testament to the enduring legacy of Metrodorus of Lampsacus, whose ideas continue to inspire and challenge scholars and philosophers to this day.
